proofs.proof_tex:
Put \(b=\|\beta(P)\|_2\), \(c=\check\theta(P)\), and
\[
 r=\alpha(P)-c\beta(P).
\]
The phrase \emph{the reduced-form primitives are defined} includes \(b>0\), because the displayed definition of \(\check\theta(P)\) divides by \(b^2\).  That definition gives \(\beta(P)^{\prime}r=0\).  Consequently, by the Pythagorean identity,
\[
 \begin{split}
 q_P(\theta)
 &=\|r+(c-\theta)\beta(P)\|_2^2-\tau^2\\
 &=\|r\|_2^2+b^2(\theta-c)^2-\tau^2
 =b^2(\theta-c)^2-\delta(P). \tag{1}
 \end{split}
\]
The published reduction in \(\mathrm{def:watson\mbox{-}published\mbox{-}reduction}\) identifies the causal target with the observed-law sublevel set in (1); thus this equality is not imposed by definition in the present proof.  If \(\delta(P)<0\), (1) is strictly positive for every real \(\theta\), and hence \(\Theta_I(P)=\varnothing\).  If \(\delta(P)\geq0\), division by \(b>0\) in (1) gives
\[
 q_P(\theta)\leq0
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 c-\frac{\sqrt{\delta(P)}}{b}\leq\theta\leq
 c+\frac{\sqrt{\delta(P)}}{b}.
\]
The two endpoints are exactly \(\theta_-(P)\) and \(\theta_+(P)\), so
\[
 \Theta_I(P)=K\cap[\theta_-(P),\theta_+(P)]. \tag{2}
\]
Now let \(P\in\mathcal P_W\).  Premultiplying the outcome equation in \(\mathrm{ass:outcome\mbox{-}equation}\) by \(Z_i\), taking expectations, and using \(\mathrm{ass:outcome\mbox{-}orthogonality}\) gives
\[
 \Sigma_{zy}(P)=\Sigma_{zz}(P)\gamma+\theta_0\Sigma_{zx}(P).
\]
The covariance-conditioning assumption makes \(\Sigma_{zz}(P)\) invertible.  Applying its inverse and the definitions of \(\alpha(P)\) and \(\beta(P)\) yields
\[
 \alpha(P)-\theta_0\beta(P)=\gamma. \tag{3}
\]
By \(\mathrm{ass:l2\mbox{-}leakage}\), (3) implies \(q_P(\theta_0)=\|\gamma\|_2^2-\tau^2\leq0\).  Because \(\theta_0\in K\), the structural target belongs to \(\Theta_I(P)\); in particular the set is nonempty and \(\delta(P)\geq0\).

Write \(K=[k_-,k_+]\).  If \(\theta_-(P)\leq k_-\), then (2) and nonemptiness imply \(k_-\in\Theta_I(P)\), so \(\operatorname{dist}(\Theta_I(P),\partial K)=0\), contrary to \(\mathrm{ass:parameter\mbox{-}margin}\).  Hence \(\theta_-(P)>k_-\).  The same argument at the right boundary gives \(\theta_+(P)<k_+\).  Therefore (2) has no truncation and
\[
 \Theta_I(P)=[\theta_-(P),\theta_+(P)].
\]
Both the contact class and the interior class are subclasses of \(\mathcal P_W\), so the conclusion applies on their union.

Fix \(h\in[0,\bar H]\), put \(a=a_{n,h}\), and use the specialization \(d=2\), \(\tau=1\), and \(K=[-2,2]\) from \(\mathrm{def:gaussian\mbox{-}witness}\).  Permuting coordinates from \((Z_1,Z_2,X,Y)\) to \((Z_1,X,Z_2,Y)\) turns \(\Sigma(a)\) into the block diagonal matrix
\[
 B_1=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&2\end{pmatrix},
 \qquad
 B_2(a)=\begin{pmatrix}1&a\\a&1+a^2\end{pmatrix}. \tag{1}
\]
Both determinants equal one.  The trace of \(B_1\) is three, while the trace of \(B_2(a)\) is \(2+a^2\leq3\).  For a positive \(2\)-by-\(2\) matrix of determinant one, the larger eigenvalue is increasing in its trace and the smaller one is its reciprocal.  The eigenvalues of \(B_1\) are \((3\pm\sqrt5)/2\).  Thus (1) proves
\[
 \frac{3-\sqrt5}{2}\leq\lambda_{\min}\{\Sigma(a)\}
 \leq\lambda_{\max}\{\Sigma(a)\}\leq\frac{3+\sqrt5}{2}. \tag{2}
\]
In particular \(\Sigma(a)\) is positive definite.  If \(G_4\sim N(0,I_4)\) and \(L=(3+\sqrt5)/2\), then \(W\) has the same law as \(\Sigma(a)^{1/2}G_4\), whence \(\|W\|_2^8\leq L^4\|G_4\|_2^8\).  Since \(\|G_4\|_2^2\) is chi-squared with four degrees of freedom,
\[
 E\|G_4\|_2^8=4\cdot6\cdot8\cdot10=1920,
\]
which gives the asserted eighth-moment bound.

The observable covariance blocks are \(\Sigma_{zz}=I_2\), \(\Sigma_{zx}=(1,0)^{\prime}\), and \(\Sigma_{zy}=(0,a)^{\prime}\).  Therefore
\[
 \beta=(1,0)^{\prime},\qquad
 \alpha=(0,a)^{\prime},\qquad
 \check\theta=0,
\]
and the structural representation in \(P_{n,h}\) has \(\theta_0=0\) and \(\gamma=(0,a)^{\prime}\).  Its leakage norm is \(a\leq1=\tau\), its relevance norm is one, and
\[
 \lambda(P_{n,h})=a^2,
 \qquad
 \delta(P_{n,h})=1-a^2=\frac{h}{\sqrt n}\leq\frac{C_\delta}{\sqrt n}. \tag{3}
\]
We next calculate the score variance rather than assuming it.  At this law, differentiation of the two least-squares reduced forms gives
\[
 d\alpha=Z\{Y-\alpha^{\prime}Z\}=Z\epsilon_y,
 \qquad
 d\beta=Z\{X-\beta^{\prime}Z\}=Z\epsilon_x.
\]
For \(g_\theta=\alpha-\theta\beta=(-\theta,a)^{\prime}\), differentiation of \(q_P(\theta)=\|g_\theta\|_2^2-1\) consequently yields the influence function
\[
 \psi_{P_{n,h}}(W;\theta)
 =2(-\theta Z_1+aZ_2)(\epsilon_y-\theta\epsilon_x). \tag{4}
\]
The two factors in (4) are independent centered Gaussian variables, with variances \(\theta^2+a^2\) and \(1+\theta^2\), respectively.  Hence
\[
 \sigma_{P_{n,h}}(\theta)^2
 =4(\theta^2+a^2)(1+\theta^2). \tag{5}
\]
The condition \(\sqrt n\geq2\bar H\) gives \(a^2=1-h/\sqrt n\geq1/2\).  For \(\theta\in[-2,2]\), (5) is therefore between \(2\) and \(4(4+1)(1+4)=100\).  Equations (2)--(5), together with the numerical compatibility inequalities in the witness definition, verify every covariance, moment, relevance, leakage, and score-nondegeneracy condition in \(\mathcal P_W\).

By the endpoint-domain lemma and (3),
\[
 \Theta_I(P_{n,h})=
 \left[-\sqrt{h/\sqrt n},\sqrt{h/\sqrt n}\right]. \tag{6}
\]
Moreover, \(h/\sqrt n\leq1/2\), so its distance from the boundary of \([-2,2]\) is
\[
 2-\sqrt{h/\sqrt n}\geq2-1/\sqrt2>1\geq m_K. \tag{7}
\]
Thus the parameter margin holds, no \(K\)-truncation occurs, and (3) proves \(P_{n,h}\in\mathcal P_n^{\mathrm{ct}}(C_\delta)\), uniformly in \(h\).

It remains to verify the experiment claim.  Under the reference \(P_{n,0}\), only the conditional regression of \(Y\) on \(Z_2\) changes.  With \(u_{n,h}=\sqrt n(a_{n,h}-1)\), its log likelihood ratio is exactly
\[
 \log\frac{dP_{n,h}^{\,n}}{dP_{n,0}^{\,n}}
 =u_{n,h}\Delta_n-\frac{u_{n,h}^2}{2}\,n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^nZ_{2i}^2,
 \qquad
 \Delta_n=n^{-1/2}\sum_{i=1}^nZ_{2i}\epsilon_{y,i}. \tag{8}
\]
Uniformly on the compact \(h\)-set, \(u_{n,h}=-h/2+O(n^{-1/2})\).  A Taylor expansion of the characteristic function of the centered summands \(Z_{2i}\epsilon_{y,i}\), whose variance is one and whose third absolute moment is finite, gives \(\Delta_n\Rightarrow N(0,1)\); the same moment calculation gives \(n^{-1}\sum Z_{2i}^2\to1\) in probability.  Substitution in (8) yields
\[
 \log\frac{dP_{n,h}^{\,n}}{dP_{n,0}^{\,n}}
 =-\frac h2\Delta_n-\frac{h^2}{8}+o_{P_{n,0}}(1), \tag{9}
\]
uniformly for \(h\in[0,\bar H]\).  This is the LAN expansion with local coordinate \(-h/2\).

For completeness, contiguity follows directly.  If \(\Delta a=a_{n,h}-1\), conditioning on the \(Z_{2i}\)'s in (8) gives
\[
 E_{P_{n,0}}\left[\left(\frac{dP_{n,h}^{\,n}}{dP_{n,0}^{\,n}}\right)^2\right]
 =(1-2\Delta a^2)^{-n/2}, \tag{10}
\]
which is uniformly bounded on compact \(h\)-sets because \(n\Delta a^2\to h^2/4\).  The analogous reverse likelihood ratio has the same bound.  Cauchy--Schwarz applied to either likelihood ratio shows that an event whose probability tends to zero under one sequence has probability tending to zero under the other.  This proves mutual contiguity and completes the proof.

Throughout the proof \(h\in[0,\bar H]\), \(a=a_{n,h}\), and all remainders are uniform in \(h\).  The witness-membership theorem gives \(a\to1\), \(\beta=e_1\), \(\alpha=ae_2\), \(\check\theta=0\), and \(\delta=h/\sqrt n\).

Let \(S_n=n^{-1}\sum_iW_iW_i^{\prime}\).  Since the observations are centered Gaussian with uniformly bounded moments,
\[
 \widehat\Sigma_n-\Sigma(a)
 =n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n\{W_iW_i^{\prime}-\Sigma(a)\}
   -\overline W_n\overline W_n^{\prime},
 \qquad
 \sqrt n\,\|\overline W_n\overline W_n^{\prime}\|_{\mathrm{op}}=o_P(1). \tag{1}
\]
On the event \(\lambda_{\min}(\widehat\Sigma_{zz,n})\geq m_\Sigma/2\), the resolvent identity gives
\[
 \|R_n(\widehat\Sigma_{zz,n})-
        \widehat\Sigma_{zz,n}^{-1}\|_{\mathrm{op}}
 \leq4m_\Sigma^{-2}n^{-2}. \tag{2}
\]
The fourth-moment expansion for entries of the sample covariance makes the complement of this event \(O(n^{-2})\), uniformly.  Thus (2) is \(o(n^{-1/2})\) for all first-order calculations below.

Differentiate \(\delta=1-\lambda\).  At the witness, the residual in the projection defining \(\lambda\) is \(ae_2\), which is orthogonal to \(\beta=e_1\); hence the derivative of the estimated center drops out and
\[
 \operatorname{IF}_{\delta}(W)=-2aZ_2\epsilon_y. \tag{3}
\]
The smooth covariance expansion based on (1)--(3) gives
\[
 \sqrt n\{\widehat\delta_n-h/\sqrt n\}
 =-2a\,n^{-1/2}\sum_{i=1}^nZ_{2i}\epsilon_{y,i}+o_P(1). \tag{4}
\]
The summands have mean zero, variance one before multiplication by \(-2a\), and uniformly bounded third moments.  Expanding their characteristic functions at the origin therefore gives, uniformly in \(h\),
\[
 \sqrt n\{\widehat\delta_n-h/\sqrt n\}\Rightarrow Z,
 \qquad Z\sim N(0,4). \tag{5}
\]
The center has influence function
\[
 \operatorname{IF}_{\check\theta}(W)
 =Z_1\epsilon_y+aZ_2\epsilon_x,
\]
so \(\widehat{\check\theta}_n=O_P(n^{-1/2})\), while \(\|\widehat\beta_n\|_2=1+O_P(n^{-1/2})\).  The lower truncation \(\|\widehat\beta_n\|_2\vee n^{-1}\) is consequently inactive with probability tending to one.  By the continuous mapping identity \(n^{1/4}\sqrt{(\widehat\delta_n)_+}=\sqrt{(\sqrt n\widehat\delta_n)_+}\), (5) and the definition of the total interval yield
\[
 n^{1/4}(\widehat\theta_-^{\mathrm{tot}},
          \widehat\theta_+^{\mathrm{tot}})
 \Rightarrow
 \left(-\sqrt{(h+Z)_+},\sqrt{(h+Z)_+}\right). \tag{6}
\]

Conditional on the sample, the empirical-bootstrap analogue of (4) is
\[
 \sqrt n(\widehat\delta_{n,b}^*-\widehat\delta_n)
 =n^{-1/2}\sum_{j=1}^n
 \{\widehat\varphi_{I_{bj}^*}-\overline{\widehat\varphi}\}+o_{P^*}(1), \tag{7}
\]
where \(\widehat\varphi_i=-2\widehat a\,Z_{2i}\widehat\epsilon_{y,i}\) is the plug-in version of (3).  The empirical second moment in (7) converges to four and its empirical Lindeberg remainder vanishes, uniformly in \(h\), because the Gaussian witness has moments of every order uniformly on the compact path.  Expanding the conditional characteristic function of the multinomial sum in (7) gives a conditional \(N(0,4)\) limit.  Jointly with (5), it can be represented by \(Z^*\sim N(0,4)\) independent of \(Z\).  Therefore
\[
 \sqrt n\widehat\delta_{n,b}^*\Rightarrow h+Z+Z^* \tag{8}
\]
conditionally on the contact-limit realization.  The bootstrap center is again \(O_{P^*}(n^{-1/2})\), and its bootstrap denominator converges to one.  Hence the scaled candidate upper endpoint converges conditionally to \(\sqrt{(h+Z+Z^*)_+}\), with the lower endpoint its negative.

Strict retention is the event \(\widehat\delta_{n,b}^*>0\).  Because the limiting normal variable in (8) has no mass at zero, its conditional probability converges to
\[
 p_h(Z)=P\{Z^*>-(h+Z)\mid Z\}
 =\Phi\left(\frac{h+Z}{2}\right). \tag{9}
\]
For every realized finite \(Z\),
\[
 \inf_{0\leq h\leq\bar H}p_h(Z)=\Phi(Z/2)>0. \tag{10}
\]
Let \(p_{n,h}\) be the exact conditional candidate-retention probability.  Conditional independence of the \(B_n\) candidates gives
\[
 P(M_n=0\mid W_1,\ldots,W_n)=(1-p_{n,h})^{B_n}. \tag{11}
\]
For any \(\varepsilon>0\), the right side is at most \(e^{-B_n\varepsilon}+\mathbf1\{p_{n,h}<\varepsilon\}\).  Uniform conditional convergence in (9), followed by (10), implies
\[
 \lim_{\varepsilon\downarrow0}\limsup_n
 \sup_{h\in[0,\bar H]}P_{n,h}(p_{n,h}<\varepsilon)=0.
\]
Since \(B_n\to\infty\), (11) proves \(\sup_hP_{n,h}(M_n=0)\to0\).

Finally, for any function \(f\) bounded by one, the conditional variance of the retained empirical average is bounded, on \(p_{n,h}>0\), by a constant times \((B_np_{n,h})^{-1}\).  The preceding small-\(p_{n,h}\) argument shows \(B_np_{n,h}\to\infty\) in probability uniformly.  A finite bounded-Lipschitz net, followed by its Lipschitz extension, therefore turns the conditional ratio law of large numbers into bounded-Lipschitz convergence of the empirical retained law.  Combining this fact with (8)--(9) gives
\[
 \mathcal L\!\left(\sqrt{h+Z+Z^*}\mid
 Z^*>-(h+Z),Z\right)=\mathcal K_h(Z) \tag{12}
\]
for the scaled upper coordinate, and its reflection for the lower coordinate.  Subtracting the original scaled upper endpoint in (6) changes (12) by exactly \(-\sqrt{(h+Z)_+}\).  The zero-retention fallback is negligible by (11), which completes every asserted convergence.

Let \(g(x)=\sqrt{x_+}\).  The contact endpoint proof gives the following conditional limit for the ordinary centered upper endpoint:
\[
 \mathcal O_{h,z}
 =\mathcal L\{g(h+z+Z^*)-g(h+z)\}, \tag{1}
\]
whereas its sampling limit, centered at the population endpoint, is
\[
 \mathcal S_h
 =\mathcal L\{g(h+Z)-\sqrt h\}. \tag{2}
\]
For the retained algorithm the corresponding conditional centered limit is
\[
 \mathcal R_{h,z}
 =\mathcal L\{g(h+z+Z^*)-g(h+z)\mid
 Z^*>-(h+z)\}. \tag{3}
\]
These kernels are not constant in the first-stage realization \(z\).  Put
\[
 f(x)=\min\{(-x)_+,1\}.
\]
This function is bounded by one and has Lipschitz constant one.  At \(h=0\), (2) is supported on \([0,\infty)\), so \(\int f\,d\mathcal S_0=0\).  At \(z=1\), the variable in (1) equals \(-1\) whenever \(Z^*\leq-1\); hence
\[
 \int f\,d\mathcal O_{0,1}\geq P(Z^*\leq-1)=\Phi(-1/2)>0. \tag{4}
\]
For (3), on the retained event \(-1<Z^*<-1/2\) the centered endpoint belongs to \((-1,-1+1/\sqrt2)\), and therefore
\[
 \int f\,d\mathcal R_{0,1}
 \geq (1-1/\sqrt2)
 \frac{P(-1<Z^*<-1/2)}{P(Z^*>-1)}>0. \tag{5}
\]
Normal probabilities and the integrals in (1)--(3) are continuous in \((h,z)\) near \((0,1)\); the conditioning probability in (3) is bounded away from zero there.  Thus (4)--(5) imply that there are \(h_0>0\), \(\rho>0\), and \(\varepsilon>0\) such that, for
\[
 H_0=[0,h_0]\subseteq[0,\bar H],
\]
after reducing \(h_0\) if necessary, both bounded-Lipschitz distances from (2) exceed \(2\varepsilon\) whenever \(h\in H_0\) and \(z\in[1-\rho,1+\rho]\).  The probability
\[
 \pi_0=P\{Z\in[1-\rho,1+\rho]\}
\]
is strictly positive.  Uniform conditional convergence in the contact endpoint theorem and the triangle inequality now give, for any \(0<\pi<\pi_0\),
\[
 \inf_{h\in H_0}P_{n,h}\!\left\{
 d_{\mathrm{BL}}(\widehat{\mathcal O}_{n,h},\mathcal S_h)>\varepsilon
 \right\}\geq\pi+o(1), \tag{6}
\]
and the identical assertion for the centered version of \(\widehat{\mathbb L}_n^{\mathrm{ret}}\).  Projection onto one coordinate is one-Lipschitz, so separation of the upper marginal in (6) implies separation of the endpoint-pair laws.  The retained zero-candidate fallback does not change this conclusion because its probability tends to zero uniformly by the contact endpoint theorem.

A bounded-Lipschitz separation of two probability measures on the line implies disagreement of their distribution functions at some continuity point.  Otherwise their integrals against every piecewise-linear bounded-Lipschitz approximation to an interval indicator would agree.  At such a continuity point, the left-continuous quantile maps differ on a nonempty interval of probability indices.  Equations (4)--(6) therefore show that coordinate percentile calibration based on either the ordinary conditional law or the retained quantiles \(Q_{n,-}^{\mathrm{ret}},Q_{n,+}^{\mathrm{ret}}\) has a nonvanishing coverage error along a subsequence in \(H_0\).  Hence neither the ordinary nor the feasibility-discarded percentile workflow attains uniform endpoint coverage on the contact-local class.

Let \(b=\|\beta(P)\|_2\) and \(c=\check\theta(P)\).  Fixed relevance gives \(b\geq c_\beta>0\).  The orthogonal decomposition proved in the endpoint-domain lemma gives
\[
 q_P(\theta)=b^2(\theta-c)^2-\delta(P),
 \qquad
 \Theta_I(P)=\left[c-\frac{\sqrt{\delta(P)}}b,
                         c+\frac{\sqrt{\delta(P)}}b\right], \tag{1}
\]
with no \(K\)-truncation under the parameter-margin assumption.  Let
\[
 A_r=\{\theta\in K:\widetilde q(\theta)\leq r\}.
\]
If \(A_r=\varnothing\), the convention defining \(d_{\to}\) gives zero loss and there is nothing to prove.  Otherwise the explicit uniform error bound forces \(r\geq0\), and every \(\theta\in A_r\) obeys
\[
 q_P(\theta)\leq\widetilde q(\theta)+r\leq2r.
\]
Using (1),
\[
 |\theta-c|\leq\frac{\sqrt{\delta(P)+2r}}b. \tag{2}
\]
The distance from such a point to the interval in (1) is bounded by
\[
 \left\{\frac{\sqrt{\delta(P)+2r}-\sqrt{\delta(P)}}b\right\}_+. \tag{3}
\]
If \(0\leq\delta(P)\leq C_\delta r\), (3) is at most
\[
 \frac{\sqrt{\delta(P)+2r}}b
 \leq\frac{\sqrt{C_\delta+2}}{c_\beta}\sqrt r. \tag{4}
\]
If \(\delta(P)\geq\delta_0\), rationalizing (3) instead gives
\[
 \frac{2r}{b\{\sqrt{\delta(P)+2r}+\sqrt{\delta(P)}\}}
 \leq\frac{2r}{c_\beta\sqrt{\delta_0}}. \tag{5}
\]
Taking the supremum over \(\theta\in A_r\) in (4) or (5) is exactly the outer directed-Hausdorff loss.  This proves the stated contact square-root modulus and interior linear modulus.

Put \(a=a_{\mathrm{int}}\), \(b=b_{n,t}=a+t/\sqrt n\), and use \(d=2\), \(\tau=1\), and \(K=[-2,2]\).  The first displayed condition on \(n\) gives
\[
 b\geq a-\bar T/\sqrt n\geq a/2,
 \qquad
 b\leq a+\bar T/\sqrt n\leq(1+a)/2<1. \tag{1}
\]
After the same coordinate permutation used for the contact witness,
\[
 \Sigma(b)\sim
 \begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&2\end{pmatrix}
 \oplus
 \begin{pmatrix}1&b\\b&1+b^2\end{pmatrix}. \tag{2}
\]
Both blocks in (2) have determinant one, and the second has trace \(2+b^2\leq3\).  Therefore
\[
 \frac{3-\sqrt5}{2}\leq\lambda_{\min}\{\Sigma(b)\}
 \leq\lambda_{\max}\{\Sigma(b)\}\leq\frac{3+\sqrt5}{2}. \tag{3}
\]
As in the contact calculation, if \(L=(3+\sqrt5)/2\), then
\[
 E\|W_i\|_2^8\leq L^4E\|N(0,I_4)\|_2^8=1920L^4. \tag{4}
\]
The reduced forms and structural quantities are
\[
 \beta=(1,0)^{\prime},\qquad
 \alpha=(0,b)^{\prime},\qquad
 \check\theta=\theta_0=0,\qquad
 \gamma=(0,b)^{\prime}. \tag{5}
\]
In particular relevance equals one and the leakage restriction holds because \(0<b<1=\tau\).  The score influence calculation is unchanged except that \(a\) is replaced by \(b\):
\[
 \psi(W;\theta)=2(-\theta Z_1+bZ_2)(\epsilon_y-\theta\epsilon_x),
 \qquad
 \sigma(\theta)^2=4(\theta^2+b^2)(1+\theta^2). \tag{6}
\]
By (1), the lower bound in (6) is \(4b^2\geq a^2\); on \([-2,2]\), the upper bound is at most \(100\).  The compatibility restrictions on \(c_\sigma\) and \(C_\sigma\) therefore verify score nondegeneracy.

Moreover,
\[
 \delta(P_{n,t}^{\mathrm{int}})=1-b^2
 =1-a^2-\frac{2at}{\sqrt n}-\frac{t^2}{n}. \tag{7}
\]
Uniformly for \(|t|\leq\bar T\), the second displayed restriction on \(n\) and (7) imply \(\delta(P_{n,t}^{\mathrm{int}})\geq\delta_0\).  The endpoint-domain lemma now yields
\[
 \Theta_I(P_{n,t}^{\mathrm{int}})
 =[-\sqrt{1-b^2},\sqrt{1-b^2}]\subset(-1,1), \tag{8}
\]
because \(b>0\).  Its distance to the boundary of \([-2,2]\) is strictly greater than one and hence at least \(m_K\).  Equations (1), (3)--(8), together with the structural Gaussian construction, verify all defining assumptions of \(\mathcal P_W\) and the interior-slack condition.  Thus \(P_{n,t}^{\mathrm{int}}\in\mathcal P^{\mathrm{int}}(\delta_0)\) uniformly over the full compact path.

For LAN, take \(P_{n,0}^{\mathrm{int}}\) as reference and put
\[
 \Delta_n=n^{-1/2}\sum_{i=1}^nZ_{2i}\epsilon_{y,i}.
\]
The conditional normal regression likelihood gives the exact identity
\[
 \log\frac{d(P_{n,t}^{\mathrm{int}})^n}
          {d(P_{n,0}^{\mathrm{int}})^n}
 =t\Delta_n-\frac{t^2}{2}\,n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^nZ_{2i}^2. \tag{9}
\]
The characteristic-function calculation for the centered products gives \(\Delta_n\Rightarrow N(0,1)\), and the second term in (9) converges to \(-t^2/2\), uniformly on \([-\bar T,\bar T]\).  This is LAN with information one.  Finally,
\[
 E_{P_{n,0}^{\mathrm{int}}}\left[
 \left\{\frac{d(P_{n,t}^{\mathrm{int}})^n}
 {d(P_{n,0}^{\mathrm{int}})^n}\right\}^{\!2}\right]
 =(1-2t^2/n)^{-n/2}, \tag{10}
\]
which is bounded uniformly for \(|t|\leq\bar T\) and large \(n\); the reverse ratios obey the same bound.  Cauchy--Schwarz proves mutual contiguity.

We prove the two lower bounds by explicit two-law testing calculations.  No regularity of the competing random closed set beyond the stated measurability and coverage is used.

\textbf{Contact experiment.}
Choose \(h_*\in(0,\bar H]\) sufficiently small that
\[
 v_{\mathrm{ct}}:=\frac12\sqrt{\exp(h_*^2/4)-1}<1-\eta. \tag{1}
\]
This is possible because \(\bar H>0\) and \(\eta<1/2\).  Let \(P_n=P_{n,0}\), \(Q_n=P_{n,h_*}\), and \(L_n=dQ_n^n/dP_n^n\).  The conditional Gaussian regression likelihood calculation in the contact witness proof gives, with \(\Delta a_n=a_{n,h_*}-1\),
\[
 E_{P_n}L_n^2=(1-2\Delta a_n^2)^{-n/2}
 \longrightarrow\exp(h_*^2/4). \tag{2}
\]
For every event \(A\), Cauchy--Schwarz gives the elementary total-variation bound
\[
 |Q_n(A)-P_n(A)|
 \leq\frac12E_{P_n}|L_n-1|
 \leq\frac12\sqrt{E_{P_n}L_n^2-1}. \tag{3}
\]
Choose \(\epsilon>0\) so small that \(1-\eta-\epsilon-v_{\mathrm{ct}}>0\).  If \((D_n)\in\mathfrak D_\eta^{\mathrm{ct}}\), its uniform coverage and (2)--(3) imply, for all sufficiently large \(n\),
\[
 P_n\{\Theta_I(Q_n)\subseteq D_n\}
 \geq1-\eta-\epsilon-v_{\mathrm{ct}}+o(1)=:\kappa_{\mathrm{ct}}+o(1), \tag{4}
\]
where \(\kappa_{\mathrm{ct}}>0\) after decreasing it once.

The contact witness theorem gives
\[
 \Theta_I(P_n)=\{0\},\qquad
 \Theta_I(Q_n)=[-\sqrt{h_*}\,n^{-1/4},
                 \sqrt{h_*}\,n^{-1/4}]. \tag{5}
\]
On the event in (4), \(D_n\) contains \(\sqrt{h_*}\,n^{-1/4}\).  Hence, under \(P_n\),
\[
 d_{\to}(D_n,\Theta_I(P_n))\geq\sqrt{h_*}\,n^{-1/4}. \tag{6}
\]
Taking expectations in (6) on that event proves
\[
 \sup_{h\in[0,\bar H]}E_{P_{n,h}}
 d_{\to}(D_n,\Theta_I(P_{n,h}))
 \geq\frac12\kappa_{\mathrm{ct}}\sqrt{h_*}\,n^{-1/4} \tag{7}
\]
for every sufficiently large \(n\).  This supplies \(c_{\mathrm{ct}}>0\) and the permitted \(N_{\mathrm{ct}}(D)\).

\textbf{Interior experiment.}
Choose \(s\in(0,\bar T]\) sufficiently small that
\[
 v_{\mathrm{int}}:=\frac12\sqrt{\exp(s^2)-1}<1-\eta. \tag{8}
\]
Let \(P_n=P_{n,0}^{\mathrm{int}}\), \(Q_n=P_{n,-s}^{\mathrm{int}}\), and let \(L_n=dQ_n^n/dP_n^n\).  The exact conditional regression likelihood now has coefficient difference \(-s/\sqrt n\), so
\[
 E_{P_n}L_n^2=(1-2s^2/n)^{-n/2}\longrightarrow e^{s^2}. \tag{9}
\]
Repeating (3)--(4), using interior-honest coverage, gives a constant \(\kappa_{\mathrm{int}}>0\) such that
\[
 P_n\{\Theta_I(Q_n)\subseteq D_n\}\geq\kappa_{\mathrm{int}} \tag{10}
\]
for all sufficiently large \(n\).

Write \(r_0=\sqrt{1-a_{\mathrm{int}}^2}\) and
\[
 r_{n,-s}=\sqrt{1-(a_{\mathrm{int}}-s/\sqrt n)^2}.
\]
The interior witness-membership theorem makes both sets untruncated and gives
\[
 r_{n,-s}-r_0
 =\frac{2a_{\mathrm{int}}s/\sqrt n-s^2/n}
        {r_{n,-s}+r_0}
 \geq\frac{a_{\mathrm{int}}s}{2\sqrt n} \tag{11}
\]
for sufficiently large \(n\), since both radii are at most one.  On the event in (10), \(D_n\) contains \(r_{n,-s}\), while the right endpoint of \(\Theta_I(P_n)\) is \(r_0\).  Thus
\[
 d_{\to}(D_n,\Theta_I(P_n))
 \geq r_{n,-s}-r_0.
\]
Combining this inequality with (10)--(11) proves
\[
 \sup_{t\in[-\bar T,\bar T]}E_{P_{n,t}^{\mathrm{int}}}
 d_{\to}(D_n,\Theta_I(P_{n,t}^{\mathrm{int}}))
 \geq\frac{\kappa_{\mathrm{int}}a_{\mathrm{int}}s}{2}\,n^{-1/2}. \tag{12}
\]
The quantified restrictions on \(n\) are precisely those under which the interior witness theorem certifies class membership; enlarging \(N_{\mathrm{int}}(D)\) enforces them.  Finally, the adaptive score-hull theorem supplies upper risks of orders \(n^{-1/4}\) and \(n^{-1/2}\) under the same loss.  Equations (7) and (12) therefore establish the two matched minimax frontiers.

Fix \(P\in\mathcal P^{\mathrm{int}}(\delta_0)\).  By definition, \(\delta(P)\geq\delta_0>0\), and fixed relevance gives \(\|\beta(P)\|_2\geq c_\beta>0\).  The endpoint-domain lemma and the parameter margin consequently give
\[
 \Theta_I(P)=[\theta_-(P),\theta_+(P)]
\]
without \(K\)-truncation.

On the open neighborhood of \(\Sigma(P)\) on which \(\lambda_{\min}(\Sigma_{zz})>m_\Sigma/2\), \(\|\beta\|_2>c_\beta/2\), and \(\delta>\delta_0/2\), the maps
\[
 \Sigma\longmapsto
 \alpha=\Sigma_{zz}^{-1}\Sigma_{zy},\quad
 \Sigma\longmapsto
 \beta=\Sigma_{zz}^{-1}\Sigma_{zx},\quad
 (\alpha,\beta)\longmapsto
 \check\theta=\frac{\beta^{\prime}\alpha}{\|\beta\|_2^2}
\]
are continuously differentiable.  So are
\[
 \lambda=\|\alpha-\check\theta\beta\|_2^2,\qquad
 \delta=\tau^2-\lambda,\qquad
 \theta_\pm=\check\theta\pm\frac{\sqrt\delta}{\|\beta\|_2}, \tag{1}
\]
because every divisor in (1) is bounded away from zero.  This establishes the claimed differentiability rather than assuming it.

For fixed \(P\), the characteristic-function expansion applied to
\[
 n^{-1/2}\sum_{i=1}^n
 \operatorname{vech}\{W_iW_i^{\prime}-\Sigma(P)\}
\]
gives a multivariate Gaussian limit, since the eighth-moment assumption supplies the required second and third moments.  The centering correction satisfies \(\sqrt n\,\overline W_n\overline W_n^{\prime}=o_P(1)\).  Taylor expansion of the continuously differentiable map (1) therefore yields
\[
 \sqrt n\left\{
 (\widehat\theta_-^{\mathrm{tot}},\widehat\theta_+^{\mathrm{tot}})
 -(\theta_-(P),\theta_+(P))\right\}
 \Rightarrow N(0,V_P), \tag{2}
\]
where \(V_P\) is the covariance obtained by applying the derivative of (1) to the covariance influence vector.  The Gaussian law may be degenerate.  The positive-part convention is inactive with probability tending to one because \(\widehat\delta_n\to\delta(P)\geq\delta_0\), and the ridge resolvent difference is \(O(n^{-2})=o(n^{-1/2})\) on an event with probability tending to one.  Thus (2) applies to the stated totalized endpoints.

Finally, the affirmative multiplier-coupling theorem and the interior branch of the adaptive score-hull theorem give
\[
 E_Pd_{\to}(C_n,\Theta_I(P))=O(n^{-1/2}).
\]
Hence the contact-robust construction retains the ordinary root-\(n\) Gaussian endpoint behavior and root-\(n\) outer set loss at every fixed interior law.

theorem.proof_tex:
We give a finite-dimensional proof tailored to the quadratic score.  Let \(m=(d+2)(d+3)/2\), let \(\operatorname{vech}\) be any fixed isometry from symmetric \((d+2)\)-by-\((d+2)\) matrices into \(\mathbb R^m\), and set
\[
 V_{i,P}=\operatorname{vech}\{W_iW_i^{\prime}-\Sigma(P)\},
 \qquad
 S_{n,P}=n^{-1/2}\sum_{i=1}^nV_{i,P}. \tag{1}
\]
Assumption \(\mathrm{ass:iid\mbox{-}centered}\) gives \(E_PV_{i,P}=0\).  The eighth-moment bound implies
\[
 \sup_{P\in\mathcal P_W}E_P\|V_{i,P}\|_2^4<\infty. \tag{2}
\]
Covariance conditioning makes every population \(\Sigma_{zz}(P)\) invertible with inverse norm at most \(m_\Sigma^{-1}\).  On the fixed neighborhood in which the instrument block has smallest eigenvalue at least \(m_\Sigma/2\), differentiating the inverse explicitly shows that the first two derivatives of \(S\mapsto\mathfrak q_n(S;\theta)\) are bounded uniformly in \(\theta\in K\), \(P\in\mathcal P_W\), and large \(n\).  Since \(q_P(\theta)\) is quadratic in \(\theta\), its first derivative can be written
\[
 \psi_P(W_i;\theta)=a_P(\theta)^{\prime}V_{i,P},
 \qquad
 a_P(\theta)=a_{0,P}+a_{1,P}\theta+a_{2,P}\theta^2, \tag{3}
\]
where the three coefficient vectors are uniformly bounded.  This follows directly from
\[
 D\{A^{-1}b\}[H]=A^{-1}(h-H_AA^{-1}b)
\]
and \(D\|u\|_2^2[du]=2u^{\prime}du\).

The centered covariance satisfies
\[
 \widehat\Sigma_n-\Sigma(P)
 =n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n\{W_iW_i^{\prime}-\Sigma(P)\}
   -\overline W_n\overline W_n^{\prime}. \tag{4}
\]
Fourth-moment expansion using (2) gives
\[
 \sup_P E_P\|\widehat\Sigma_n-\Sigma(P)\|_{\mathrm F}^4=O(n^{-2}),
 \qquad
 \sup_P E_P\|\overline W_n\|_2^8=O(n^{-4}). \tag{5}
\]
Define
\[
 \mathcal E_{n,P}=\{\lambda_{\min}(\widehat\Sigma_{zz,n})\geq m_\Sigma/2\}.
\]
Equations (5), the variational eigenvalue inequality, and Markov's inequality show
\[
 \sup_PP(\mathcal E_{n,P}^c)=O(n^{-2}). \tag{6}
\]
Taylor's formula, (4)--(5), and the resolvent bound for the \(n^{-2}\) ridge give on \(\mathcal E_{n,P}\)
\[
 \sup_{\theta\in K}\left|
 \sqrt n\{\widehat q_n(\theta)-q_P(\theta)\}
 -a_P(\theta)^{\prime}S_{n,P}\right|=\rho_{n,P},
 \qquad
 \sup_PE_P[\rho_{n,P}\mathbf1_{\mathcal E_{n,P}}]=O(n^{-1/2}). \tag{7}
\]
This is the particular linearization also guaranteed by \(\mathrm{lem:ridge\mbox{-}totalization\mbox{-}negligible}\).

Formula (3) and its sample analogue show that \(\widehat\psi_i(\theta)\) is a polynomial of degree at most two in \(\theta\).  Let \(\Omega_P=E_P[V_{i,P}V_{i,P}^{\prime}]\).  Expanding the finitely many empirical coefficients and using (2) yields
\[
 \sup_{\theta\in K}|\widehat\sigma_n^2(\theta)-
 a_P(\theta)^{\prime}\Omega_Pa_P(\theta)|=o_P(1) \tag{8}
\]
uniformly over \(P\in\mathcal P_W\).  The left side restricted to \(\mathcal E_{n,P}\) is bounded in \(L^2\) by \(Cn^{-1/2}\).  Score nondegeneracy and (8) imply
\[
 P\!\left\{\inf_{\theta\in K}\widehat\sigma_n(\theta)
 \geq c_\sigma/2\right\}\longrightarrow1 \tag{9}
\]
uniformly.  Thus the \(n^{-1}\) denominator truncation is asymptotically inactive.

Conditional on the sample, \(\widehat{\mathbb G}_n^\xi(\theta)\) is a centered Gaussian polynomial of degree at most two in \(\theta\).  After division by its empirical standard deviation, it has the representation
\[
 \frac{\widehat{\mathbb G}_n^\xi(\theta)}
      {\widehat\sigma_n(\theta)\vee n^{-1}}
 =u_n(\theta)^{\prime}G_n, \tag{10}
\]
where \(G_n\) is standard Gaussian in a space of dimension at most three and \(\|u_n(\theta)\|_2\leq1\).  Consequently
\[
 0\leq\widehat c_{1-\eta}
 \leq Q_{1-\eta}\{\|N(0,I_3)\|_2\}=:c_\eta<\infty. \tag{11}
\]
The lower inequality uses \(1-\eta>1/2\) and the fact that the supremum dominates one centered unit-variance Gaussian coordinate on the event in (9); only the upper bound is needed elsewhere.

We now prove uniform conditional approximation by contradiction.  If it failed, there would be a sequence \(P_n\in\mathcal P_W\) along which failure had probability bounded away from zero.  The covariance matrices \(\Omega_{P_n}\), the three bounded vectors in (3), and the finitely many coefficients of \(\sigma_{P_n}^2(\theta)\) lie in compact Euclidean sets.  Pass to a subsequence on which they converge.  For every fixed \(t\in\mathbb R^m\), (2) permits the uniform characteristic-function expansion
\[
 E_{P_n}\exp\{it^{\prime}V_{i,P_n}/\sqrt n\}
 =1-\frac{t^{\prime}\Omega_{P_n}t}{2n}+O(n^{-3/2}). \tag{12}
\]
Raising (12) to the \(n\)-th power proves that \(S_{n,P_n}\) converges to a centered Gaussian vector with the limiting covariance.  The empirical covariance of the coefficient vector in (10) converges in probability to the same limiting covariance: each entry is an average of a polynomial of degree at most four in \(W_i\), and its variance is bounded by the eighth-moment assumption.  The sample coefficient vectors converge to their population counterparts by (4)--(5).  Thus, conditionally on the data, the Gaussian vector driving (10) converges to the same limit as the vector in (12).

The map taking a coefficient vector to the supremum over compact \(K\) is continuous under uniform convergence of the three polynomial coefficients and the studentizer; \(c_\sigma>0\) prevents division by zero.  Along the selected subsequence,
\[
 d_{\mathrm{BL}}\!\left(
 \mathcal L_{P_n}(T_{n,P_n}),
 \mathcal L_\xi(T_n^\xi\mid W_1,\ldots,W_n)
 \right)\longrightarrow0 \tag{13}
\]
in \(P_n\)-probability.  This contradicts the supposed failure and proves (13) uniformly over the class.

For quantile transfer, every subsequential Gaussian limit has the form
\[
 H(G)=\sup_{\theta\in K}v(\theta)^{\prime}G,
 \qquad \|v(\theta)\|_2=1, \tag{14}
\]
on its effective Gaussian support.  Its \((1-\eta)\)-quantile is at least \(\Phi^{-1}(1-\eta)>0\), since (14) dominates any fixed \(v(\theta_0)^{\prime}G\).  Write \(G=RU\), with \(R\) independent of the uniform direction \(U\).  Conditional on every direction for which \(H(U)>0\), the variable \(RH(U)\) has a continuous radial density; directions with \(H(U)=0\) cannot create an atom at a positive value.  Hence (14) has no atom at its positive \((1-\eta)\)-quantile.  Compactness of the coefficient limits turns this subsequential observation into uniform upper-quantile continuity.  Combining it with (13) gives
\[
 \liminf_n\inf_{P\in\mathcal P_W}P\{T_{n,P}\leq
 \widehat c_{1-\eta}\}\geq1-\eta. \tag{15}
\]
The supremum in (15) ranges over all \(K\), so replacing it by the smaller set \(\Theta_I(P)\) proves (A).

On \(\mathcal E_{n,P}\), define
\[
 R_{n,P}=n^{-1/2}
 +\sup_{\theta\in K}|\widehat q_n(\theta)-q_P(\theta)|
 +n^{-1/2}\widehat c_{1-\eta}^{+}
   \sup_{\theta\in K}\{\widehat\sigma_n(\theta)\vee n^{-1}\}; \tag{16}
\]
on \(\mathcal E_{n,P}^c\), set \(R_{n,P}=n^{-1/2}\).  Equations (2), (5), (7)--(8), and (11) give
\[
 \sup_PE_PR_{n,P}=O(n^{-1/2}). \tag{17}
\]
The same calculations with squares show \(\sup_{n,P}E_P[(\sqrt nR_{n,P})^2]<\infty\); therefore the displayed family is uniformly integrable.

If \(\theta\in C_n\), its defining inequality and positivity of the denominator imply
\[
 \widehat q_n(\theta)
 \leq n^{-1/2}\widehat c_{1-\eta}^{+}
       \{\widehat\sigma_n(\theta)\vee n^{-1}\}.
\]
Adding the uniform score error shows \(q_P(\theta)\leq R_{n,P}\) on \(\mathcal E_{n,P}\).  The first term in (16) gives \(R_{n,P}\geq n^{-1/2}\).  This proves (B)--(C), and the proof is uniform over \(\mathcal P_W\), hence also over both named subclasses.

proofs.proof_tex:
Write \(A=\Sigma_{zz}(P)\), \(\widehat A_n=\widehat\Sigma_{zz,n}\), and \(\rho_n=n^{-2}\).  All constants below may depend on the fixed dimension \(d\), the compact interval \(K\), and the constants defining \(\mathcal P_W\), but not on \(P\in\mathcal P_W\) or \(n\).

\textbf{1. A fourth-moment covariance bound.}
Because \(A\) is a principal submatrix of \(\Sigma(P)\), assumption \(\mathrm{ass:covariance\mbox{-}conditioning}\) and the variational characterization of the smallest eigenvalue give
\[
 \lambda_{\min}(A)\geq m_{\Sigma}.
\]
Let \(A_n^0=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n Z_iZ_i^{\prime}\) and \(\overline Z_n=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n Z_i\).  The centering convention in the definition of \(\widehat\Sigma_n\) gives
\[
 \widehat A_n=A_n^0-\overline Z_n\overline Z_n^{\prime}.
\]
For fixed coordinates \(j,k\), put \(U_i^{jk}=Z_{ij}Z_{ik}-E_P[Z_{ij}Z_{ik}]\).  By Cauchy--Schwarz and assumption \(\mathrm{ass:eighth\mbox{-}moment}\),
\[
 \sup_{P\in\mathcal P_W}E_P|U_i^{jk}|^4<\infty.
\]
Independence and centering imply, by expanding the fourth power and retaining only index patterns in which every index occurs at least twice,
\[
 E_P\left|n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^nU_i^{jk}\right|^4
 =n^{-4}\left\{nE_P[(U_1^{jk})^4]+3n(n-1)E_P[(U_1^{jk})^2]^2\right\}
 \leq Cn^{-2}.
\]
Since \(d\) is fixed, equivalence of matrix norms therefore yields
\[
 \sup_{P\in\mathcal P_W}E_P\|A_n^0-A\|_{\mathrm{op}}^4\leq Cn^{-2}. \tag{1}
\]
Similarly, expansion of the eighth power of each coordinate of \(\overline Z_n\) has at most four distinct indices in every nonzero term: any index occurring exactly once makes that term vanish by assumption \(\mathrm{ass:iid\mbox{-}centered}\).  H\"older's inequality and the uniform eighth-moment bound thus give
\[
 \sup_{P\in\mathcal P_W}E_P\|\overline Z_n\|_2^8\leq Cn^{-4}. \tag{2}
\]
Using \(\|vv^{\prime}\|_{\mathrm{op}}=\|v\|_2^2\), equations \((1)\)--\((2)\), and \((a+b)^4\leq8(a^4+b^4)\), we obtain
\[
 \sup_{P\in\mathcal P_W}E_P\|\widehat A_n-A\|_{\mathrm{op}}^4\leq Cn^{-2}. \tag{3}
\]
For symmetric matrices, the variational formula gives directly
\[
 \lambda_{\min}(\widehat A_n)
 \geq \lambda_{\min}(A)-\|\widehat A_n-A\|_{\mathrm{op}}.
\]
Consequently, Markov's inequality and \((3)\) imply
\[
 \begin{split}
 \sup_{P\in\mathcal P_W}P\{\lambda_{\min}(\widehat A_n)<m_{\Sigma}/2\}
 &\leq \sup_{P\in\mathcal P_W}P\{\|\widehat A_n-A\|_{\mathrm{op}}>m_{\Sigma}/2\}\\
 &\leq (2/m_{\Sigma})^4\sup_{P\in\mathcal P_W}E_P\|\widehat A_n-A\|_{\mathrm{op}}^4
 \leq Cn^{-2}. \tag{4}
 \end{split}
\]
This proves the asserted uniform probability bound.

\textbf{2. Resolvent and smooth-score comparisons.}
Let \(E_n=\{\lambda_{\min}(\widehat A_n)\geq m_{\Sigma}/2\}\).  On \(E_n\), both \(T_0=\widehat A_n^{-1}\) and \(T_{\rho}=(\widehat A_n+\rho_n I_d)^{-1}\) exist, and
\[
 \|T_0\|_{\mathrm{op}}\leq 2/m_{\Sigma},
 \qquad
 \|T_{\rho}\|_{\mathrm{op}}\leq 2/m_{\Sigma}.
\]
The resolvent identity, proved by multiplying both sides by \(\widehat A_n+\rho_n I_d\) and \(\widehat A_n\), is
\[
 T_{\rho}-T_0=-\rho_nT_{\rho}T_0.
\]
It follows that, on \(E_n\),
\[
 \|R_n(\widehat\Sigma_{zz,n})-\widehat\Sigma_{zz,n}^{-1}\|_{\mathrm{op}}
 \leq \frac{4n^{-2}}{m_{\Sigma}^2}. \tag{5}
\]

We next make the comparison with the inverse-defined objects explicit.  For a generic covariance matrix \(S\), write \(A_S=S_{zz}\), \(b_{x,S}=S_{zx}\), \(b_{y,S}=S_{zy}\),
\[
 b_{\theta,S}=b_{y,S}-\theta b_{x,S},\qquad
 T_{r,S}=(A_S+rI_d)^{-1},\qquad
 u_{r,S}(\theta)=T_{r,S}b_{\theta,S},
\]
and
\[
 f_{r,S}(\theta)=\|u_{r,S}(\theta)\|_2^2-\tau^2.
\]
Thus, at \(S=\widehat\Sigma_n\), the choice \(r=\rho_n\) gives the ridge-defined reduced forms and score, whereas \(r=0\) gives their inverse-defined versions on \(E_n\).  Since \(K\) is compact, \(M_K=\sup_{\theta\in K}|\theta|<\infty\).  The eighth-moment assumption implies uniformly that
\[
 \|\widehat\Sigma_n\|_{\mathrm{op}}=O_P(1). \tag{6}
\]
Indeed, the square of its operator norm is bounded, up to a fixed-dimensional constant, by a sample average of \(\|W_i\|_2^4\) plus \(\|\overline W_n\|_2^4\), whose expectations are uniformly bounded.

Equations \((5)\)--\((6)\) now give
\[
 \|\widehat\beta_n-\widetilde\beta_n\|_2
 +\|\widehat\alpha_n-\widetilde\alpha_n\|_2
 =O_P(n^{-2}) \tag{7}
\]
uniformly over \(\mathcal P_W\), where tildes denote inverse-defined versions on \(E_n\), with any measurable extension on \(E_n^c\).  The identity
\[
 |\|x\|_2^2-\|y\|_2^2|
 \leq (\|x\|_2+\|y\|_2)\|x-y\|_2
\]
and \((6)\)--\((7)\) then yield
\[
 \sup_{\theta\in K}|\widehat q_n(\theta)-\widetilde q_n(\theta)|=O_P(n^{-2}). \tag{8}
\]

For completeness, the derivative comparison needed for the influence process follows from a direct differentiation, rather than from an unstated smoothness assertion.  For a symmetric perturbation \(H\), set \(h_\theta=H_{zy}-\theta H_{zx}\).  Differentiating the inverse identity gives \(D T_{r,S}[H]=-T_{r,S}H_{zz}T_{r,S}\), and hence
\[
 D_Sf_{r,S}(\theta)[H]
 =2u_{r,S}(\theta)^{\prime}T_{r,S}
   \{h_\theta-H_{zz}u_{r,S}(\theta)\}. \tag{9}
\]
On \(E_n\cap\{\|\widehat\Sigma_n\|_{\mathrm{op}}\leq M\}\), formula \((9)\), the resolvent identity, and the triangle inequality imply for a constant \(C_M<\infty\)
\[
 \sup_{\theta\in K}
 \|D_Sf_{\rho_n,\widehat\Sigma_n}(\theta)
      -D_Sf_{0,\widehat\Sigma_n}(\theta)\|_{\mathrm{op}}
 \leq C_Mn^{-2}. \tag{10}
\]
No division beyond the inverses controlled in \((5)\) occurs in this step.

Put
\[
 H_{i,n}=(W_i-\overline W_n)(W_i-\overline W_n)^{\prime}-\widehat\Sigma_n.
\]
The fourth-moment consequence of assumption \(\mathrm{ass:eighth\mbox{-}moment}\) gives
\[
 n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n\|H_{i,n}\|_{\mathrm F}^2=O_P(1) \tag{11}
\]
uniformly.  Applying \((10)\) to \(H_{i,n}\), then using \((6)\) and \((11)\), proves
\[
 \sup_{\theta\in K}
 \left[n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n
   \{\widehat\psi_i(\theta)-\widetilde\psi_i(\theta)\}^2
 \right]^{1/2}
 =O_P(n^{-2})=o_P(n^{-1/2}). \tag{12}
\]
The reverse triangle inequality for Euclidean norms also gives
\[
 \sup_{\theta\in K}|\widehat\sigma_n(\theta)-\widetilde\sigma_n(\theta)|
 \leq
 \sup_{\theta\in K}
 \left[n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n
   \{\widehat\psi_i(\theta)-\widetilde\psi_i(\theta)\}^2
 \right]^{1/2}
 =O_P(n^{-2}). \tag{13}
\]

We record why studentization is uniformly safe.  Formula \((9)\) shows that, as a function of \(\theta\), each inverse-defined influence score is a polynomial of degree at most two.  Its squared value is therefore a polynomial of degree at most four.  The finitely many empirical coefficients of these polynomials are continuous functions of \(\widehat\Sigma_n\) and sample averages of products of at most four coordinates of \(W_i\).  Their variances are uniformly bounded by assumption \(\mathrm{ass:eighth\mbox{-}moment}\).  Entrywise Chebyshev bounds, \((3)\), and compactness of \(K\) consequently imply
\[
 \sup_{\theta\in K}|\widetilde\sigma_n(\theta)-\sigma_P(\theta)|=o_P(1) \tag{14}
\]
uniformly over \(P\in\mathcal P_W\).  Assumption \(\mathrm{ass:score\mbox{-}nondegeneracy}\), \((13)\), and \((14)\) imply that, with probability tending to one uniformly,
\[
 \inf_{\theta\in K}\{\widehat\sigma_n(\theta)\wedge\widetilde\sigma_n(\theta)\}
 \geq c_{\sigma}/2. \tag{15}
\]
Thus the truncation by \(n^{-1}\) in both critical-value formulas is inactive for all sufficiently large \(n\) on this event.

\textbf{3. Stability of the conditional Gaussian quantile.}
Let
\[
 v_r(\theta)=\bigl(D_Sf_{r,\widehat\Sigma_n}(\theta)[H_{1,n}],\ldots,
 D_Sf_{r,\widehat\Sigma_n}(\theta)[H_{n,n}]\bigr)^{\prime},
 \qquad
 a_r(\theta)=\frac{v_r(\theta)}{\|v_r(\theta)\|_2}.
\]
On the event in \((15)\), these vectors are well defined for \(r\in\{0,\rho_n\}\), and
\[
 \frac{n^{-1/2}\sum_{i=1}^n\xi_iD_Sf_{r,\widehat\Sigma_n}(\theta)[H_{i,n}]}
 {(n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^nD_Sf_{r,\widehat\Sigma_n}(\theta)[H_{i,n}]^2)^{1/2}}
 =\xi^{\prime}a_r(\theta). \tag{16}
\]
Equations \((12)\)--\((15)\) and the elementary normalization inequality
\[
 \left\|\frac{x}{\|x\|_2}-\frac{y}{\|y\|_2}\right\|_2
 \leq \frac{2\|x-y\|_2}{\|y\|_2}
\]
give
\[
 e_n:=\sup_{\theta\in K}\|a_{\rho_n}(\theta)-a_0(\theta)\|_2=O_P(n^{-2}) \tag{17}
\]
uniformly.  By \((9)\), \(v_r(\theta)\) is a vector-valued polynomial of degree at most two.  Hence all vectors in
\[
 \mathcal A_r=\{a_r(\theta):\theta\in K\}
\]
belong to a subspace of dimension at most three, and \(\mathcal A_0\cup\mathcal A_{\rho_n}\) belongs to a subspace of dimension at most six.  Conditional on the data, the two suprema in the critical values are therefore support functions of compact subsets of the unit sphere evaluated at one standard Gaussian vector \(G\in\mathbb R^r\), where \(1\leq r\leq6\).

We now prove the needed quantile continuity in this fixed dimension.  Fix \(p=1-\eta>1/2\).  For a nonempty compact \(\mathcal A\subseteq\mathbb S^{r-1}\), let
\[
 X_{\mathcal A}=\sup_{a\in\mathcal A}a^{\prime}G.
\]
For any \(a_0\in\mathcal A\),
\[
 a_0^{\prime}G\leq X_{\mathcal A}\leq\|G\|_2,
\]
so its \(p\)-quantile lies between \(z_p=\Phi^{-1}(p)>0\) and the \(p\)-quantile of \(\|N(0,I_6)\|_2\).  Write \(G=RU\), where \(R=\|G\|_2\) and \(U\) is uniform on the unit sphere and independent of \(R\).  On the spherical cap \(\{a_0^{\prime}U\geq1/2\}\), whose probability is bounded below uniformly over \(1\leq r\leq6\),
\[
 1/2\leq \sup_{a\in\mathcal A}a^{\prime}U\leq1.
\]
The radial density is continuous and bounded below on every compact subinterval of \((0,\infty)\).  Conditioning on this cap therefore proves that constants \(c_p>0\) and \(s_p>0\), depending only on \(p\) and the bound \(r\leq6\), satisfy
\[
 P\{x<X_{\mathcal A}\leq x+s\}\geq c_ps \tag{18}
\]
whenever \(0<s\leq s_p\) and \(x\) lies in a fixed compact interval containing every such \(p\)-quantile.  The same polar representation shows that \(X_{\mathcal A}\) has no atom at a positive point.

If compact \(\mathcal A,\mathcal B\subseteq\mathbb S^{r-1}\) have Euclidean Hausdorff distance at most \(e\), then
\[
 |X_{\mathcal A}-X_{\mathcal B}|\leq e\|G\|_2. \tag{19}
\]
For sufficiently small \(e\), choose \(u_e=C e\sqrt{\log(1/e)}\), with \(C\) large enough that
\[
 P\{e\|G\|_2>u_e\}\leq e^2
\]
uniformly for \(r\leq6\).  Apply \((18)\) at the \(p\)-quantile of \(X_{\mathcal B}\), with \(s=2e^2/c_p\), and use \((19)\).  This gives
\[
 Q_p(X_{\mathcal A})\leq Q_p(X_{\mathcal B})+u_e+2e^2/c_p.
\]
Interchanging \(\mathcal A\) and \(\mathcal B\) proves
\[
 |Q_p(X_{\mathcal A})-Q_p(X_{\mathcal B})|
 \leq C_p e\sqrt{\log(1/e)}. \tag{20}
\]
Thus \((16)\)--\((17)\) and \((20)\) yield
\[
 |\widehat c_{1-\eta}-\widetilde c_{1-\eta}|
 =O_P(n^{-2}\sqrt{\log n})=o_P(n^{-1/2}) \tag{21}
\]
uniformly over \(\mathcal P_W\).  This derivation also shows, under the same coupling of multipliers,
\[
 E_{\xi}\left[
 \sup_{\theta\in K}|\xi^{\prime}a_{\rho_n}(\theta)-\xi^{\prime}a_0(\theta)|
 \mathrel{\big|}W_1,\ldots,W_n\right]
 \leq \sqrt6\,e_n=O_P(n^{-2}),
\]
which is the asserted first-order equivalence of the standardized multiplier influence processes.

The same covariance argument applies conditionally to an empirical-bootstrap resample.  Conditional on the data, its eighth-moment envelope is \(n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n\|W_i\|_2^8=O_P(1)\).  Repeating the fourth-moment expansion conditionally shows, on \(E_n\), that the conditional probability that the resample instrument covariance is more than \(m_{\Sigma}/4\) away from \(\widehat A_n\) is \(O_P(n^{-2})\).  On the complementary conditional event its smallest eigenvalue is at least \(m_{\Sigma}/4\), and the preceding resolvent and derivative calculations apply with changed constants.  Hence ridge totalization is also asymptotically immaterial for the empirical-bootstrap weak limits.

Equations \((7)\), \((8)\), \((12)\), and \((21)\), together with \((4)\), establish the claimed uniform \(o_P(n^{-1/2})\) equivalence.  For the positive-part endpoint maps, the only nonsmooth operation additionally satisfies
\[
 |\sqrt{x_+}-\sqrt{y_+}|\leq\sqrt{|x-y|},
\]
so the \(O_P(n^{-2})\) score perturbation contributes only \(O_P(n^{-1})\) at quadratic contact, which is negligible after \(n^{1/4}\) scaling; away from contact the ordinary Lipschitz bound is even sharper.  Thus all stated contact and interior weak limits are unchanged.

\textbf{4. Expected-loss contribution of the fallback event.}
The target set is nonempty under the structural restrictions.  Indeed, assumptions \(\mathrm{ass:outcome\mbox{-}equation}\) and \(\mathrm{ass:outcome\mbox{-}orthogonality}\) give
\[
 \Sigma_{zy}(P)=\Sigma_{zz}(P)\gamma+\theta_0\Sigma_{zx}(P),
 \qquad
 \alpha(P)=\gamma+\theta_0\beta(P).
\]
Because \(\theta_0\in K\) and assumption \(\mathrm{ass:l2\mbox{-}leakage}\) gives \(\|\gamma\|_2\leq\tau\),
\[
 q_P(\theta_0)=\|\gamma\|_2^2-\tau^2\leq0,
 \qquad
 \theta_0\in\Theta_I(P).
\]
Let \(D_K=\operatorname{diam}(K)<\infty\).  For every closed \(A\subseteq K\), including \(A=\varnothing\), the definition of the directed loss and nonemptiness of \(\Theta_I(P)\) imply
\[
 0\leq d_{\to}(A,\Theta_I(P))\leq D_K.
\]
Therefore the contribution of the near-singular event to any stated expected outer-loss bound is at most
\[
 D_KP(E_n^c)=O(n^{-2}),
\]
uniformly over \(P\in\mathcal P_W\).  This is negligible relative to both \(n^{-1/4}\) and \(n^{-1/2}\), completing the proof.
